cards.title: Use the Value Equation to Diagnose a Product Offer
cards.summary: Increase a product offer’s perceived value by improving the desired outcome and confidence while reducing wait time and customer effort.
cards.use_when: Designing a product bundle, subscription, or product-page promise that shoppers currently compare mainly by price.
steps: Assess the offer through four variables: Dream Outcome multiplied by Perceived Likelihood of Achievement, divided by Time Delay multiplied by Effort and Sacrifice.

For the dream outcome, state the end benefit the product helps deliver rather than only its specifications. For example, a cookware set may promise simpler weeknight meals, provided that claim is supportable.
Raise perceived likelihood with concrete product proof: compatible-use guidance, customer reviews, demonstrations, quality details, credible guarantees, and precise claims.
Reduce time delay with inventory visibility, realistic delivery timing, immediate digital access where applicable, or a product configuration that helps customers start sooner.
Reduce effort and sacrifice through preselected kits, clear variant guidance, simple setup instructions, replenishment options, and fewer decisions at checkout.
Score all four levers before adding a discount. Repair the weakest credible lever, then evaluate conversion and contribution margin.
caveats: Perceived value is subjective; validate the diagnosis through customer questions, reviews, behavior, and tests rather than internal assumptions.
Do not make outcome claims that the product, fulfillment, or evidence cannot support.

cards.title: Create a Category-of-One Product Bundle
cards.summary: Escape direct price comparison by packaging a distinct, credible outcome rather than selling an interchangeable item alone.
cards.use_when: Merchandising a commodity-like product category where shoppers can easily compare your SKU, price, and shipping terms with competitors.
steps: Map the common category promise and the standard components competitors sell. Identify where customers still face an unresolved job, risk, or decision.
Build a differentiated merchandise proposition around a specific outcome, such as a complete starter kit, a use-case-based collection, a more useful configuration, or a supported replenishment plan.
Make the package visibly distinct on the collection and product pages: name the use case, show what is included, explain why each component belongs, and state who it is for.
Price the complete offer on its own value and economics rather than automatically undercutting single-item competitors. Use proof, clear contents, and risk reversal to justify any premium.
Review competitor moves periodically. If a bundle element becomes standard, improve the configuration or customer experience rather than relying on an old differentiation claim.
caveats: A distinct package cannot compensate for weak demand, poor product quality, or an unbelievable outcome.
A higher price needs real, understandable customer value; novelty alone can look like inflated packaging.
cards.source_name: $100M Offers_ How To Make Offers So Good People Feel Stupid Saying No.docx

cards.title: Build Product Bundles With Trim and Stack
cards.summary: Turn the obstacles customers face into a focused bundle of product components, guidance, and add-ons that are valuable to buyers and economical to fulfill.
cards.use_when: Creating kits, gift sets, starter bundles, or subscription tiers to raise average order value without adding low-value fulfillment complexity.
steps: List the problems a customer must solve before they can get the desired result from the category. For a skincare routine, this may include selecting compatible products, knowing sequence, and maintaining replenishment.
Convert each problem into a candidate solution: a product, accessory, guide, sampling format, or replenishment option that removes that obstacle.
Choose the lowest-cost delivery form that genuinely helps. A printed insert, QR-linked usage guide, or preconfigured kit may solve a problem more efficiently than a costly physical add-on.
Trim components that add substantial sourcing, packing, shipping, or return complexity but do little to improve the buyer’s progress.

Stack the retained components as one coherent named bundle. On the PDP, explain the role of each item and show the bundle price versus purchasing the relevant items separately when that comparison is accurate.
Track bundle take rate, contribution margin, return reasons, and repeat purchase so the stack improves both shopper value and store economics.
caveats: Evaluate cost against customer-perceived value, not warehouse effort alone.
Do not stack unrelated extras merely to make a bundle look larger; they can obscure the core purchase decision and create fulfillment errors.

cards.title: Choose an Ecommerce-Appropriate Guarantee Structure
cards.summary: Select unconditional, conditional, or no-refund terms based on product controllability, return exposure, and the specific buyer risk you need to reduce.
cards.use_when: Writing return, satisfaction, fit, delivery, or product-support terms for a PDP, cart, or checkout where hesitation centers on wasting money.
steps: Identify the exact risk preventing purchase: product quality, fit, compatibility, shipment reliability, or uncertainty about use.

Use an unconditional return or satisfaction guarantee when you can operationally absorb returns and want the strongest risk reversal. State the refund window, condition requirements, and process plainly.

Use a conditional guarantee when the outcome depends on defined customer actions or a measurable store obligation. For example, make a compatibility promise contingent on the shopper using the published compatibility checker correctly.
Use a service guarantee for controllable operations, such as replacing a damaged shipment or resolving an error under clear conditions.
A no-refund position is a selective option, not a default. If used for an eligible product class, explain the commitment rationale and make terms highly conspicuous before checkout.
Ensure the PDP, cart, checkout, customer-service macros, and policy pages use the same terms.
caveats: Model return shipping, product disposition, fraud, and support costs before strengthening a guarantee.
Product-category rules, payment-provider requirements, and consumer law may limit what return or no-refund terms you can use; verify applicable requirements.

cards.title: Evaluate Guarantee Economics With Net Contribution
cards.summary: A stronger guarantee is worthwhile only when incremental orders produce more contribution than refunds, returns, and associated fulfillment costs consume.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to add or expand a return, satisfaction, replacement, or make-good promise for an ecommerce product offer.
steps: Set a baseline using purchase conversion rate, average order value, product cost, pick-pack and shipping cost, payment fees, return rate, refund amount, and contribution margin.

Specify the guarantee change and its expected effect as a test hypothesis, not a certainty. The source uses a service-sales illustration in which a large close-rate increase outweighed a 10% refund rate; that result is not an ecommerce benchmark.
Run a controlled test where feasible, or compare a clearly defined pre/post period while accounting for traffic source, seasonality, and inventory changes.
Calculate net contribution: additional completed orders and retained revenue minus incremental refunds, return shipping, reverse-logistics losses, replacements, support, and fraud.

Set a review threshold appropriate to the store’s economics. If return reasons reveal preventable mismatch, improve PDP guidance, sizing, compatibility information, or product quality before simply narrowing the policy.
Monitor results after launch because return behavior can lag initial purchase conversion.
caveats: Do not use lead conversion or sales-call close-rate examples as if they were purchase-conversion benchmarks.
A guarantee cannot sustainably overcome a product that routinely disappoints customers.

cards.title: Use Truthful Urgency for Product Launches and Promotions
cards.summary: Give shoppers a real reason to act now through dated launches, seasonal windows, expiring offer terms, or genuinely time-sensitive inventory opportunities.
cards.use_when: Planning a product drop, preorder, seasonal campaign, or time-bound bundle when customers tend to postpone a decision.
steps: Choose one urgency mechanism tied to a real operational fact. For a cohort-style launch, open a limited-run drop or preorder on stated dates; for seasonal urgency, tie the offer to a recurring relevant period.
For price or bonus urgency, set a real deadline after which the price changes or a specific add-on is removed. Configure storefront, ads, email, and support information to match it.
For an exploding opportunity, use only external or inventory constraints that genuinely will not recur, such as a one-time collaboration allocation or event-specific package.
Place the deadline near the purchasing decision on the landing page, PDP, cart, and campaign emails, while preserving the full offer terms elsewhere.
Honor the stated end date. After the campaign, remove or update countdowns, offer bars, bonuses, and automated messages.
Review whether urgency increased completed purchases without increasing cancellations, returns, or customer complaints.
caveats: Repeatedly extended or fabricated deadlines undermine trust and may create compliance risk.
Urgency is not a substitute for a clear product fit, credible value, and available inventory.

cards.title: Apply Honest Scarcity to Inventory and Bonuses
cards.summary: Use real limits on inventory, production capacity, or a defined bonus allocation to communicate availability without creating false pressure.
cards.use_when: Merchandising a limited product run, constrained seasonal inventory, made-to-order capacity, or first-buyer bonus during a launch.
steps: Identify the constrained resource: units on hand, production slots, preorder capacity, or a limited quantity of a specific bonus item.
State the limit precisely where possible, such as available units or the number of gift-with-purchase items. Ensure the number is tied to inventory or fulfillment data.
Keep the core product available if appropriate while limiting only a genuinely constrained bonus for the first stated number of buyers.
Use “will not return” or “never available again” language only when the exact package, product, or price truly will not be offered again.
Synchronize the scarcity message across ads, PDPs, cart, checkout, email, and customer support. Remove the claim once inventory is replenished or the cap is reached.
Audit fulfillment so the store does not oversell the capped item or quietly reset the claimed limit.
caveats: False scarcity damages reputation and can prompt complaints; caps must be enforced rather than silently restarted.
Layering many countdowns, low-stock notices, and bonus caps at once can make a legitimate limit appear manufactured.

cards.title: Name a Bundle So Shoppers Understand It Immediately
cards.summary: Use the M-A-G-I-C naming elements—Magnet, Avatar, Goal, Interval, and Container—to make a kit or promotion easier to understand and remember.
cards.use_when: Naming a product kit, collection, seasonal promotion, subscription tier, or replenishment program for a specific customer use case.
steps: Draft the Magnet: the hook or reason the package exists, such as seasonal preparation, travel convenience, or a limited-edition collaboration.
Name the Avatar when segmentation clarifies buying relevance, such as first-time home bakers or carry-on travelers.
State the Goal in shopper language: the result the products help them accomplish, not a vague label such as “premium set.”
Add an Interval only if it is truthful and useful, such as a seven-day travel kit or a 30-day replenishment supply. Do not imply a product outcome will occur within that period without support.
Choose the Container: kit, set, system, box, bundle, or another format that accurately describes what is sold.
Combine only the elements needed for clarity. For example, “30-Day Sensitive Skin Starter Kit” identifies a duration, audience, and format without forcing every element into the title.
Test the name with a cold reader: they should be able to tell who it is for, what it supports, and what is included after seeing the name and short subtitle.
caveats: Forcing all five elements into every name can create awkward, overly long titles.
The title must match actual contents, supply duration, and realistic product use.

cards.title: Maintain Offer Congruence From Ad Through Post-Purchase
cards.summary: Keep price, contents, incentives, guarantee, and deadline consistent across every customer touchpoint so shoppers do not discover conflicting terms after clicking or buying.
cards.use_when: Launching or changing a promotion, bundle, bonus, guarantee, or pricing structure across paid acquisition, storefront, checkout, and lifecycle email.
steps: Create a single offer record containing product or variant, price, contents, bundle savings method, bonus, shipping treatment, guarantee, eligibility, inventory limit, and deadline.
Use that record to check the acquisition ad, landing page or PDP, cart drawer, checkout copy, confirmation page, transactional emails, and scheduled campaign flows.
Remove expired offer banners, old creative, discontinued bonuses, stale product descriptions, and automated emails that still mention previous terms.
Check that urgency and scarcity claims agree. A page cannot credibly say both “unlimited availability” and “only 20 left” for the same item without a clear distinction.
Assign an owner and a launch/change checklist so merchandising, paid media, email, and support update together.
After deployment, place a test order and inspect the customer-facing experience end to end, including any discount logic and confirmation messaging.
caveats: Congruence is baseline operational hygiene rather than differentiation by itself.
Evergreen landing pages, cached ad creative, and automated lifecycle flows are common sources of stale terms; verify the current platform interfaces and publishing status.
cards.source_name: $100M Offers_ How To Make Offers So Good People Feel Stupid Saying No.docx

cards.title: Use Anchors and Decoys to Guide Bundle Choice
cards.summary: Present a credible premium reference and well-structured tiers so the intended product bundle has a clearer value context without changing its actual price.
cards.use_when: Structuring a collection, bundle selector, subscription tier page, or product comparison table where shoppers struggle to choose among options.
steps: Choose the package you want most suitable shoppers to select, then define the shopper need it best serves.
Place a genuinely higher-value, higher-priced tier nearby as an anchor. Make its additional products, capacity, service, or convenience visible so its price is credible.
Where appropriate, offer a lower or decoy configuration that is meaningfully less suitable for the target use case, making the preferred package’s incremental value easy to see.
Keep comparison dimensions consistent: quantity, product contents, supply period, compatibility, shipping treatment, and price. Avoid hiding material differences.
Use clear visual hierarchy to recommend the target option, but let shoppers select other tiers without obstruction.

Measure package mix, revenue per session, contribution margin, return rate, and complaints—not merely clicks on the highlighted tier. Revise if the premium anchor causes confusion or shifts buyers toward low-margin options.
caveats: Absurd or dishonest reference prices and staged-looking tiers reduce credibility.
Anchor effects differ by category and audience; test instead of assuming a pricing layout will work.

cards.title: Design Bonuses That Remove Purchase Obstacles
cards.summary: Use relevant, economical bonuses to resolve a real barrier to using the main product instead of discounting its list price.
cards.use_when: Improving a product launch, bundle, or cart incentive when shoppers understand the main item but hesitate over setup, selection, compatibility, or missing accessories.
steps: Review product questions, support tickets, cart abandonment feedback, and reviews to identify obstacles that prevent customers from buying or using the main item successfully.
Match each meaningful obstacle to a bonus with a clear job. Examples include a compatible accessory, a product-use guide, a sample, a care item, or early access to a needed replenishment option.
Give the bonus a specific name and describe its function. If presenting a standalone value, use an amount customers could realistically pay for that item rather than an invented inflated figure.
Set a deadline or quantity cap only when the bonus is genuinely limited by inventory, supplier terms, or campaign timing.
Show the main product first, then position the bonus as support for the core result. Keep redemption and fulfillment instructions simple.
Calculate incremental product, packing, shipping, and return costs. Remove bonuses that create little buyer value or operationally costly order complexity.
caveats: Too many bonuses can hide the main product and make the offer harder to fulfill.
A bonus should not be used to mask unclear product fit or an unsupported outcome promise.

cards.title: Gate Offer Changes With Contribution Margin
cards.summary: Approve discounts, bundles, bonuses, guarantees, and shipping incentives only after evaluating their effect on net contribution, not conversion or revenue alone.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a proposed ecommerce offer change before it reaches paid traffic, email subscribers, or the storefront.
steps: Establish the current unit economics for the affected product or bundle: realized selling price, discounts, product cost, packaging, pick-pack, outbound shipping subsidy, payment fees, support cost, returns, and contribution margin.
Model the proposed change. A bundle may lift average order value but add shipping weight; a bonus may improve conversion but consume inventory; a guarantee may add reverse-logistics exposure.
Estimate the conversion and order-mix change as hypotheses, then calculate the sales volume needed for the change to improve total contribution rather than only gross revenue.
Set up reporting before launch for purchase conversion, average order value, units per order, contribution per order, refund or return rate, fulfillment cost, and repeat purchase where relevant.
Run a bounded test when possible and compare against a valid baseline. Keep traffic-source mix, stock status, and seasonal demand in view.
Reject or revise a change that produces more orders but lower total contribution, unless the store has an explicit, tested retention or lifetime-value rationale.
caveats: Some acquisition offers intentionally accept lower first-order margin; that is a strategic decision that requires evidence rather than an accidental outcome.
Lifetime-value assumptions do not justify indefinite losses unless cohort behavior validates them.
